description: Composite figure of nine fracture-surface images of the low-temperature-rolled δ-ferrite steel R650, mixing optical (OM) and SEM modalities; no axes or plotted data. (a, b) are OM micrographs, each with a 10 µm scale bar, of the deformed zone of the impact fracture: alternating light/dark lamellar bands run roughly along the rolling direction and terminate at a dark fracture void; (a) also carries ND/RD orientation arrows. (c) is an OM image (10 µm bar) of the tensile-fracture deformed zone, showing a stepped, serrated delamination profile. (d–g) are SEM images (10 µm bars) of the impact fracture: (d) a black arrow marks a blunted crack tip surrounded by torn deformation ridges; (e) labels a "Crack" with an arrow and, inside a white dashed box, a "Secondary crack"; (f) white arrows mark "Microvoids and microcracks" aligned along the lamellae; (g) (5 µm bar) a dashed box outlines a band of microvoids/particles along a lamella. (h, i) (5 µm bars) are SEM views of the tensile fracture in which black arrows mark cracks running parallel to the lamellar orientation within δ-ferrite, surrounded by numerous fine bright spherical particles. The figure's argument: lamellar carbide/ferrite interfaces blunt, deflect and channel cracks into long paths, giving the crack-propagation resistance behind the reported toughness.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is an optical micrograph with a 10 µm scale bar and ND/RD orientation arrows, showing alternating bright and dark lamellar bands running along RD and terminating at a dark fracture void.
Panel (b) is an optical micrograph with a 10 µm scale bar showing a large dark fracture void bordered by lamellar bands (impact-fracture deformed zone).
Panel (c) is an optical micrograph with a 10 µm scale bar of the tensile-fracture deformed zone, showing a stepped/serrated delamination profile.
In panel (d), a black arrow points to a blunted crack tip embedded in heavily torn deformation ridges (SEM, 10 µm scale bar).
In panel (e), a black arrow labelled "Crack" points to a crack while a white dashed rectangle is labelled "Secondary crack" (SEM, 10 µm scale bar).
In panel (f), white arrows labelled "Microvoids and microcracks" point to microvoids and microcracks arranged in rows parallel to the lamellae (SEM, 10 µm scale bar).
In panel (g), a white dashed rectangle outlines a band of microvoids/particles running along a lamella (SEM, 5 µm scale bar).
In panels (h) and (i) (SEM, 5 µm scale bars), black arrows mark cracks confined within lamellae and running parallel to the lamellar orientation, surrounded by numerous fine spherical particles.
The caption states that panels (a, b) and (c) are OM images and (d–g) and (h, i) are SEM images, with (a, b, d–g) from impact fracture surfaces and (c, h, i) from tensile fracture surfaces of R650.
The citing text states that the crack tip in Fig. 8d became significantly blunted and stopped propagating while penetrating the carbide/ferrite lamellae.

The citing text states that spherical carbides act as nucleation sites for microvoids (Fig. 8f) and that these secondary defects propagate mainly along the horizontal direction of the lamellae (Fig. 8g).

The citing text states that the tested steel contained numerous submicron carbides with diameter <250 nm, most spherical and distributed in the ferrite lamellae, alternating with δ-ferrite lamellae, with a small amount as short rod-like cementite at ferrite grain boundaries.

The citing text states that crack propagation was confined within δ-ferrite lamellae and ran parallel to the lamellar orientation (Fig. 8h–i) and that the tensile fracture surfaces displayed a typical serrated morphology with delamination characteristics (Fig. 8c).
No numeric data values, axis ticks or legends are printed in any panel; the only printed numbers are the scale-bar lengths (10 µm and 5 µm).

measured_quantities: scale bar length (µm) — 10 µm in panels (a)–(f), 5 µm in panels (g)–(i)
carbide diameter (nm) — <250 nm, stated in citing text, not printed on the figure
unreadable_items: panel (b): internal detail of the large dark fracture void is low-contrast and only partially resolvable
